title: Run engines, stoves and heaters without CO poisoning
summary: Carbon monoxide kills many people after disasters, usually from generators and heaters run indoors. Keep fuel-burning things outside or properly vented, fit a salvaged CO alarm in every sleeping area, and know the symptoms.

materials.item: Battery-powered CO alarm, from an abandoned home, hotel or flat

steps.text: Put generators and engines outside, at least 6 m from doors, windows and vents, with the exhaust pointing away from buildings and tents.
steps.warn: Garages, sheds, basements, porches and tarp shelters are not outside, even with the door open.

steps.text: Never run a charcoal grill, barbecue, camp stove, patio heater or generator inside a home, tent or vehicle.

Carry ashes and "dead" charcoal outside in a metal can with a metal lid, and leave them outside. Ash and coals that look out can still give off CO and heat (CPSC grill, Low Quebec ashes). Stand the can on bare ground or concrete, at least 1 m from anything else, and wait at least 7 days before you empty it (Low Quebec ashes). Never bring coals, ash or a grill indoors, or into a tent or vehicle, for warmth (CPSC charcoal, CPSC grill).
steps.warn: People die every year burning charcoal indoors, including campers and hunters trying to keep warm in tents, trucks and vans (CPSC charcoal).

steps.text: Indoors, cook and heat only with appliances made for indoor use. Vented ones, with a flue or chimney to the outside, come first. An unvented heater is acceptable only if its label allows use in a home, such as a 1-K kerosene heater, and only with a door open to the rest of the house or a window open, and a working CO alarm (CPSC 5052). See [reading a heater's label](#guides/reference_heater_labels).
steps.warn: A flue blocked by soot, nests, snow or debris pushes fumes back into the room. Check it before lighting.

steps.text: During and after a snowstorm, walk round outside and clear snow from furnace, water heater, stove and fireplace vents and from dryer vents (Health Canada CO, TSSA vents, Technical Safety BC cold). Use a brush or broom, not a shovel (TSSA vents). Side-wall vents can sit as low as 30 cm off the ground, so drifts and shovelled snow bury them (TSSA vents). Check a running generator too: keep it 6 m or more from doors, windows and vents, in a spot snow can't reach (Health Canada CO, CDC winter).
steps.warn: A buried vent pushes fumes back inside. If the alarm sounds or anyone feels ill in or after a storm, get everyone outside first, then dig.

steps.text: Leave a fresh-air opening whenever anything burns indoors, and check the flame. Blue and steady is good. Lazy, yellow and sooty means it is short of air.
Find CO alarms in abandoned homes, hotels and flats. They are often combined with smoke alarms and say CO or carbon monoxide on the label. Check the date on the back: most sensors last 5–10 years.
Fit fresh batteries, press the test button and listen for the alarm. Mount one in every sleeping area, not right beside the stove or heater.

Know what the alarm can't tell you. The test button checks the electronics, not the sensor (First Alert test). Many alarms are rated for 4.4 to 37.8 °C only, so keep them out of unheated garages, porches and attics (Kidde Nighthawk, First Alert CO710). They stay quiet at low steady levels of CO (First Alert CO710).
steps.warn: A quiet alarm doesn't mean clean air. If anyone has a headache, dizziness or nausea, get outside whatever the alarm says.

steps.text: Learn the symptoms: headache, dizziness, nausea, tiredness, confusion. If several people or pets feel ill at once, or people feel better outside, assume CO.
If the alarm sounds or anyone has symptoms, get everyone outside into fresh air at once. Turn off the source only if you can do it quickly. Don't go back in until the place has aired out.
steps.warn: Don't send someone back in to search. Open doors and windows from outside first.

steps.text: Don't sleep in a vehicle with the engine running, or in a room with an unvented heater on.

Stuck in snow in a vehicle: stay in it if it is safe from traffic, and clear snow from the tailpipe first (Transport Canada winter, CCOHS winter). Check the pipe before every restart and after any new drift (CDC MMWR, GoC winter storms). Run the engine only about 10 minutes each hour, with one window open a crack on the side away from the wind (CCOHS winter, CDC winter, Transport Canada winter). Switch it off between runs.
steps.warn: A blocked tailpipe can fill the car with CO fast. Clear just the pipe: heavy shovelling or pushing in bitter cold can be deadly (Transport Canada winter).

notes:
## Why it's so dangerous

CO sticks to the blood far more tightly than oxygen does, so even small amounts in the air steadily starve the body of oxygen. At high levels it kills within minutes. At low levels it builds up over hours. Sleeping people don't notice.

## Fuel-burning things indoors

| Source | Risk in a closed room |
|---|---|
| Petrol generator or engine | Deadly within minutes |
| Charcoal or barbecue | Very high; keeps making CO as it smoulders |
| Camp stove or gas oven used as a heater | High |
| Unflued gas or paraffin heater | High without a fresh-air opening |
| Wood stove with a clear, sound flue | Low |

## CO alarms

- A CO alarm is not a smoke alarm, though some do both. Read the label.
- Sensors wear out. Many alarms chirp or show an end-of-life warning after 5–10 years. Treat an expired one as unreliable.
- The test button checks the alarm's electronics, power and horn. It doesn't use real CO, so it can't show the sensor still works (First Alert test). An alarm that fails the test must be replaced (First Alert CO710).
- Many alarms are rated for 4.4 to 37.8 °C (40 to 100 °F). Don't mount one in an unheated garage, porch, attic or crawl space (Kidde Nighthawk, First Alert CO710). Cold can also weaken the battery and make it chirp (Kidde temperature).
- Alarms are built not to sound at a steady 30 ppm of CO. First Alert says its alarm typically does not detect CO below 30 ppm, and Kidde says its alarm has not been investigated for detection below 70 ppm (First Alert CO710, Kidde Nighthawk). CSA 6.19 also tests that an alarm stays quiet at 30 ppm for 30 days (Intertek CSA 6.19).
- At higher levels, UL 2034 alarms must sound within 4 to 15 minutes at 400 ppm, 10 to 50 minutes at 150 ppm and 60 to 240 minutes at 70 ppm (First Alert CO710). A quiet alarm is not proof of clean air: 100 ppm for 4 hours can cause headaches (First Alert CO710). Trust symptoms as well.
- Test with the button every week, and replace batteries before winter.

## Common mistakes

- Running a generator in a garage with the door open.
- Bringing a barbecue inside to keep warm.
- Pulling the battery out of a beeping alarm.
- Assuming you would smell it. You won't.
- Letting snow bury a vent or a tailpipe (Health Canada CO, CDC MMWR).
- Carrying ash or "dead" charcoal indoors for warmth (CPSC grill).
